How to sell in Milwaukee

Selling a Milwaukee house comes down to choosing a route. An agent can list it, you can market it yourself, or a cash buyer can purchase it with no repairs asked. Condition, city orders against the property and your own deadline usually settle the question.

Milwaukee has 562,407 residents, and just 41.8 percent of its housing units are lived in by owners. Expect plenty of the properties on the market to be rentals, duplexes and investor-held buildings. Owner-occupied homes carried a median value of $184,000 over 2020 to 2024, so one big repair bill can eat a large part of the price.

Flats, duplexes and tenants in place

Older brick is common here, and many blocks are lined with Polish flats, which are two-family houses with one unit above the other. An owner may occupy the upper unit and rent the lower one. An heir may inherit a flat with tenants still inside. Either way, buyers will read the leases, so decide early whether the tenants stay.

Leases, rent rolls and city registration records should be in a folder before the first buyer calls. Cash buyers will purchase a duplex with tenants in it, or a house with open orders, without asking you to fix anything. Put every offer in writing, then subtract your mortgage payoff, city charges and closing costs to see what you would really receive.

Short-term guest stays are a separate matter. DNS administers the state tourist rooming house license for stays shorter than a month, and an owner ending that use files a surrender form.

What the city checks

Most local checks run through the Department of Neighborhood Services (DNS). The department urges a DNS title search with every Milwaukee real estate transaction. The search form reveals pending code violations, special charges and city programs tied to the property, and whoever buys inherits any violation that was never abated.

  • Property registration. DNS requires registration of commercial property and of residential property nobody owner-occupies. Owner-occupied one-family, two-family and condo units are generally exempt. Use the Seller Notification Form (DNS-8D) to tell DNS ownership has changed, and call (414) 286-8569 with questions.
  • Vacant buildings. Thirty days of vacancy triggers registration. The buyer registers within 30 days of purchase, and your job as seller is to tell the buyer clearly that this is required. Putting up a For Sale sign does not cancel the duty.
  • Estates. Probate property that sits vacant is exempt when the personal representative or executor lives in the seven-county area around Milwaukee.
  • Open orders. Violations are posted in the DNS Land Management System. Call the section that issued an order to ask about it.

Nothing is charged for the first six months of vacant building registration, and DNS lists fees for renewals after that.

What Wisconsin requires of the seller

Wis. Stat. 709.02 reaches owners of buildings with one to four units. Your real estate condition report has to get to the buyer inside 10 days of your signing the accepted contract. If it is late, the buyer gets two more business days to cancel. Estate sellers get a break: a court-appointed fiduciary who never lived in the house is excused.

Under Wis. Stat. 77.22 the grantor, meaning you, pays 30 cents of transfer fee per $100 of value. Exemptions appear in section 77.25, for example a transfer from parent to child for nominal consideration or a transfer by will. File the return online with the Department of Revenue, and expect the register of deeds to take the fee when it records the deed.

Deed recording downtown

The county's deed office sits at 901 N. 9th Street, Room 103, run by the Register of Deeds. A flat $30 buys recording for one document, long or short, and the transfer fee printed on your e-RETR receipt is added to it. Bring cash, a check or a money order, because the counter takes no cards.

  1. Ask a title company or an attorney for the deed itself. The register's staff cannot draft or review one.
  2. Submit the electronic return to the Department of Revenue and print your receipt.
  3. Deliver or mail the original deed, receipt and payment.

Expect your document to be recorded in three to five business days, in the order it arrives, and the original to reach you by mail one to two weeks after that. The office phone is (414) 278-4005.

Assessments and tax bills

Revaluation of the whole city is typical every year at the Milwaukee Assessor's Office. Open Book takes place in the spring, and the assessor's website carries the next schedule. Look up any parcel at assessments.milwaukee.gov or phone the assessor at (414) 286-6565.

A missed payment earns interest at 1 percent a month. Closing agents split the current year's bill between buyer and seller, so ask yours how that will work.

Steps from first call to closing

Taking things in this sequence keeps surprises small.

  1. Order the DNS title search so no open violation or special charge surprises you.
  2. Settle whether the building counts as vacant and, if so, whether an exemption fits.
  3. With tenants in the building, collect leases, rent rolls and registration records.
  4. Request the payoff figure from your lender.
  5. Have every buyer write down a closing date and the fees that would come out of your proceeds.
  6. Fill in the condition report the moment a contract is signed. Ten days goes quickly.
  7. File the transfer return, then record the deed.
  8. Before closing, ask the title company which tax and utility balances need to be paid off.

Choosing a cash sale removes showings and buyer financing from the list. You still owe the report, the return and the recording.

Selling an inherited Milwaukee house

Heirs often sell Milwaukee flats they did not choose to own. Three rules matter most. A personal representative or executor who lives within the seven-county area around Milwaukee can leave a vacant probate property off the vacancy registration list. A court-appointed fiduciary who never lived there does not have to complete the condition report. And a transfer made by will carries no state transfer fee.

Before you set a timetable, confirm with the probate court or an attorney who holds authority to sign. A buyer's title company will ask the same question, and the deed needs the right signatures before the register accepts it. A cash buyer can often work around an unfinished basement or a roof that needs help, but nobody can work around missing authority.

Frequently asked questions

Is a title search from the city mandatory?

The city urges one on every sale but does not make it a legal requirement. It lists open violations, special charges and registration duties, which helps you and the buyer.

Who is responsible for the state transfer fee?

You are, as the grantor, at 30 cents per $100 of value under Wis. Stat. 77.22. It is collected at recording, and a transfer by will owes nothing.

Must a vacant house be registered before I sell it?

Yes, after 30 days or more of vacancy unless an exemption fits. A listing does not excuse it, and the buyer registers within 30 days of closing.

How quickly does the county record a deed?

Within three to five business days, in the order documents arrive. The original comes back by mail in one to two weeks.

Do I owe a buyer a condition report?

On most one-to-four unit homes, yes, within 10 days after the contract is accepted. A fiduciary who never occupied the home is exempt under Wis. Stat. 709.01.

What if the Madison house has been a short-term rental?

A buyer cannot take over your permit. The ZTRHP permit is issued to one host for one dwelling unit and cannot be transferred. Guests staying fewer than 30 nights make a rental short-term in the city's eyes, and state law calls the arrangement a tourist rooming house. Airbnb or VRBO listings should be closed, and the buyer should know the permit ends with you.

Rules for permit holders:

  • The unit has to be the host's primary dwelling during the rental and for the 12 consecutive months before it began.
  • While the host is away, the rental can run no more than 30 days per licensing year, July 1 to June 30.
  • Guest limits are the smaller of twice the legal bedrooms or 12 people, with children under 12 not counted.
  • A $300 one-time application fee applies, and renewal costs $100 a year.
  • Violations bring fines of $500 to $1,000 per day and possible revocation.

The host also needs a Transient Room Tax permit from the city Finance Department and a license from Public Health Madison and Dane County, and the ZTRHP permit is withheld until both exist. Before you list, ask Building Inspection to confirm your permit status in writing.

A sale does not move tenants out, so the buyer gets the lease along with the maintenance record. Use Open Book to fix facts like room counts or a permit that was unfinished on January 1. When the facts are right but the number is wrong, file an objection with the Board of Assessors. Almost every sale triggers two state rules. Wis. Stat. 77.22 puts a transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value on the seller, and Wis. Stat. 709.02 makes the seller of a one-to-four unit property furnish a condition report.

  • A fiduciary appointed by a court who never lived there need not file the report.
  • The Department of Revenue's exemptions include transfers by will or descent, foreclosure deeds to the lender and transfers between spouses.
  • Reporting a false or understated value can draw a penalty of $25 or 25% of the added fee, whichever is greater.

Even an as-is cash buyer receives the report, and the return still gets filed.

Checklist before closing

  • Deliver the condition report on time and keep proof of when it went out.
  • Have the return completed and the receipt ready for the deed package.
  • Ask for tax and payoff figures so the closing agent can prepare a settlement statement.

Cash buyers go through the same list, though without a lender's appraisal and underwriting the calendar is shorter.

Recording the deed in Dane County

Recording at the Dane County Register of Deeds costs $30 per document and requires an Electronic Transfer Return receipt. The deed names grantor and grantee, bears the grantor's notarized signature, gives the legal description and the tax bill's parcel number, and shows a return address. Only the original with original signatures is accepted. Photocopies are refused.

Mailing is possible: send the package to PO Box 1438, Madison, WI 53701-1438, with the recording fee and any transfer fee combined on a single check. Questions go to (608) 266-4141. An attorney or title company usually drafts the deed, because the office cannot complete one for you.

Will the buyer get my short-term rental permit in Madison?

No. It belongs to a specific host and unit and cannot be transferred. A buyer who wants to host guests applies separately and must meet the primary-dwelling rule.

The seller. Wis. Stat. 77.22 sets 30 cents per $100 of value, collected at recording. Transfers by will or between spouses are among the exemptions.

Which Green Bay projects need a permit, and what if I skipped one?

Tour the house with a notepad and record what you know about the roof, foundation, plumbing and wiring, since known defects go on the form. A clear list also lets a cash buyer name a firm price instead of guessing.

Estates get a break. A personal representative, trustee or conservator appointed by a court is excused when they never lived in the house, and so is any transfer that the transfer fee does not reach. A closing attorney or title company can say whether you qualify.

Getting the house ready for buyers

Buyers repeat the same questions, so have answers waiting. Photographs of the roof, basement walls and mechanical equipment taken before you list give you a record of their condition on the day you describe them on the form. Gather invoices for work on the roof, gutters and furnace, the items winter inspections focus on. Find your lender's contact information so a payoff figure can be ordered early, and keep your newest tax bill nearby for the parcel number and paid-to date.

Heading to a cash buyer? A brief written list of known problems lets them quote a firm price. Planning to list? A walk-through with an agent shows which small repairs pay off and which a buyer would sooner price in.

From contract to closing day

Several tasks run at once after signing. The title company orders its search, you deliver the condition report inside 10 days, and the electronic transfer return is readied for both signatures. A borrower waits for an appraisal and the lender's final sign-off. With cash, the closing date mostly depends on a clean title search.

On the closing date you sign the deed, which travels to the Register of Deeds together with the return receipt, and the payoff and your share of taxes are deducted from what you receive. Keep a copy of every page you sign for later reference. A short call to the register's office a day or two ahead, to confirm hours and what to bring, avoids a wasted trip downtown.

Cash sale or listing: which fits?

Weigh time, condition and certainty. A house in good shape and a seller with patience may do best on the open market. A pressing repair bill, a tenant, an estate or a firm move date points to cash, which gives up some price in return for speed and a fixed closing day.

Get each buyer to state in writing what they will pay, who covers closing costs, and how soon they can close. Lined up together, those answers show which route leaves you with more.

Selling with tenants or an inherited house

A leased house keeps its tenant until the lease ends, so read the end date and any notice terms before you name a closing day. Buyers who want the home vacant will have to settle a move-out date with the occupant, and that conversation belongs near the start of your timeline.

When a relative has died, first confirm who may sign for the estate. That person records the transfer to the heirs, which owes no fee, and then signs the later sale. Keep the two transactions separate in your notes, since each has its own return and its own recording step.

Property taxes at closing

Each side carries part of the year's tax bill at closing, with any unpaid amount taken from your proceeds. The normal pattern is two equal payments on January 31 and July 31, but a bill below $100 must be paid in full by January 31 (Wis. Stat. 74.11). A first payment that is more than five working days late after January 31 turns the whole remaining balance delinquent, and interest and penalties are charged back to the previous February 1.

Mark January 31, 2027 as the next first-installment date. Before you sign, the Kenosha County Treasurer or the city treasurer can report how much of the bill has been paid.

Only one charge is fixed by the state: the transfer fee, 30 cents for each $100 of value. Agent pay, repairs and months of carrying costs come with a listing, and most of them vanish in a cash deal. A net sheet from your title company puts both routes in numbers.

Where does the Kenosha transfer fee get paid?

At the Kenosha County Register of Deeds, when the deed is recorded. Complete the electronic return through the Department of Revenue beforehand, since the county asks for the receipt on every non-exempt conveyance.

Is it okay to sell a Kenosha house in poor repair?

Yes. Fixing it is optional, though chapter 709 sellers list known defects on the condition report. Some buyers accept the house as is and discount the work, saving you contractor visits and repair requests.

Do heirs owe the transfer fee on an inherited Kenosha house?

Not for receiving it by will or descent. Selling it afterward is a fresh conveyance and the 30 cent fee applies then. A tax professional can explain income tax on any gain.

What are the Kenosha property tax due dates?

January 31 and July 31, in two installments. A bill under $100, or a municipality with a multi-installment ordinance, changes that. A late payment can make the full remaining balance delinquent, so clear it before you list.

Selling fast in Menomonee Falls

You have three basic routes here: an agent listing, a sale on your own, or an as-is cash purchase. Each one runs into the same village and state items sooner or later. Those are the condition report, the transfer return, the last water bill and, after recent remodeling, permit sign-offs.

Menomonee Falls is a village in Waukesha County, home to 41,291 people. Roughly 74.0% of homes are lived in by their owners, and the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 was $368,000. Many buyers are therefore comparing your house with other well-kept family homes, and a clean permit history helps yours stand up.

Permits and finished work

Village rules give homeowners a lot of room to do their own projects, which means a buyer may ask who inspected the work. If you live in a one or two family home, you can handle building, indoor plumbing, heating and cooling, and most electrical jobs yourself. The service is the exception. You sign a Cautionary Statement, pull the permits and call for each inspection.

  • A contractor hired for that kind of home needs a Dwelling Contractor Certification and a Qualifier Certification from the State of Wisconsin.
  • Give the village at least 24 hours' notice before an inspection.
  • Field inspections happen between 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. After-hours visits on existing permits carry an extra charge.
  • SAFEbuilt has done the village's inspections under contract since 1985.

Did you finish a basement, deck or addition yourself? Ask the Building Inspection division whether each permit has a final inspection on file. Closing a gap now is easier than answering a buyer's inspector later. For zoning or assessing, call Community Development at (262) 532-4270.

Assessments and the Board of Review

Values are set as of January 1. During a maintenance year the number carries over unless the property itself changed, and the mail brings a Notice of Changed Assessment only to owners whose value moved. If nothing arrived, your value is the same as before.

An Open Book session takes place each fall, followed by a Board of Review meeting at Village Hall. If you want to challenge a value, go in order. Speak with the assessor informally, then file a formal objection with the Board, then, as a last step, go to Waukesha County Circuit Court. Your notice of intent has to reach the Village Clerk 48 hours or more before the Board sits. The clerk's line is 262-532-4201.

The assessor does not send or collect tax bills. Direct bill questions to the Waukesha County Treasurer.

Water, sewer and the sewer lateral

Most closings split the final water and sewer charges between buyer and seller, so a separate meter reading is rarely needed. When yours will not be split, ask the Utilities Department for a final reading and bill. Staff will want the closing date and the new owner's name. The number is (262) 532-4800.

Quarterly water bills come from three billing districts, so the dates on yours may differ from the calendar. Sewage treatment is handled regionally by the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District, which serves 28 communities.

The pipe running from your house out to the village main is the lateral, and you own it. Finding it is your task too, although village records may show its path. After a backup, crews look only at whether the main is clear. A clear main puts the next call on you, to a plumber. Take photos of the damage and write down what was lost, since that record will help you answer the sewer and water questions on the condition report.

Paperwork to pull together first

Gather these before you accept an offer, so a title company is not waiting on you.

  • The parcel number printed on your Waukesha County tax bill. It has to appear on the deed.
  • Permit and final-inspection records for work done on the house.
  • Any Notice of Changed Assessment that came from the village.
  • Water and sewer account information for the last bill.
  • If a late spouse is still on the title, form HT-110, the Termination of Decedent's Interest. The county records it for $30 together with the transfer return and a copy of the document showing the interest. This form needs no tax bill and no death certificate.

What Wisconsin asks of a seller

Under Wis. Stat. 77.22 the seller owes a transfer fee at the rate of 30 cents for every $100 of value. The Department of Revenue takes the transfer return online, and the Register of Deeds will refuse to record your deed until that return is filed.

A separate rule, Wis. Stat. 709.02, covers a house with one to four units. You owe the buyer a finished condition report no later than 10 days after the contract is accepted. Miss that window and the buyer gets 2 business days to rescind. People selling an inherited house are often excused, because a fiduciary supervised by a court who never occupied the property does not have to complete the report.

Selling to a cash buyer as-is saves you the lender appraisal and the haggling over repairs. It does not erase the report or the return.

Recording the deed and what it costs

The Waukesha County Register of Deeds records your deed. The $30 standard fee must come as a check or money order, and a transfer fee, if one applies, rides along in that same payment. Documents filed electronically come back right away. Mail in a paper deed with a stamped return envelope and plan on 2 to 3 weeks. The office answers at 262-548-7585.

Most sellers let the title company or an attorney draft the deed and handle both filings. Confirm with them how the recording fee should be paid before closing day arrives.

How the sale moves from offer to closing

Picture the order of events. First comes an accepted offer. Within 10 days the condition report goes to the buyer. While that clock runs, you or the title company file the transfer return and settle who covers any other costs. Near closing, you ask the Utilities Department about the final bill if the closing will not divide it. Then the deed is signed, recorded and the keys change hands.

An owner-occupant who did some projects personally should add one task at the start: check the permit files. A cash buyer may take the house in its current shape, but the buyer's title company will still ask for the parcel number and recorded paperwork.

Frequently asked questions

Can I do my own work on my house and still sell it?

Yes. If you live in a one or two family home, you may do your own building, indoor plumbing, heating and most electrical work after signing the Cautionary Statement, pulling permits and calling for inspections. Expect a buyer to ask whether each permit got a final inspection.

Who handles final water and sewer billing when I sell?

Call the Utilities Department at (262) 532-4800. These charges are usually split at closing, and a final reading is available if you ask. Have the closing date and the new owner's name ready.

Is the sewer lateral mine to fix?

Yes, from the house to the village main. When a backup happens, crews check the main only. If it is clear, you call a plumber.

What does the Waukesha County Register of Deeds charge to record a deed?

The standard fee is $30 per document. Pay by check or money order made out to Register of Deeds, because cash, credit and debit are refused. Any transfer fee goes in the same payment.

Do I need a condition report for an inherited house?

Not if you are a court-appointed or court-supervised fiduciary who never occupied the property. Everyone else gives the report within 10 days after the contract is accepted, as Wis. Stat. 709.02 requires.

Wausau is the county seat of Marathon County and sits on the Wisconsin River in central Wisconsin. The Census Bureau estimates 40,188 residents as of July 1, 2025, up 0.5 percent from the 39,994 counted in 2020. The wider Wausau metropolitan area, which is all of Marathon County, had 138,013 people in 2020.

What should a seller know about the city of Wausau?

Wausau grew up around logging. The Wisconsin River drew settlers in the mid-1800s, a sawmill opened in 1840, the settlement became a town by 1852, a village in 1861, and a chartered city in 1872. The railroad arrived in 1874, and by 1906 the pine was gone, so the economy shifted toward other industries, with Employers Insurance of Wausau, now part of Liberty Mutual, leading the diversification. Hmong refugees began arriving at the end of the 1970s, and Census data show 10.4 percent of residents identify as Asian alone today.

The layout is easy to explain to an out-of-town buyer. The river splits the city into east and west, with numbered streets on the east side and numbered avenues on the west side. Grand Avenue becomes North 6th Street as it enters downtown, and Business 51 follows the old route of US 51 through town. The Census Bureau counts 19.22 square miles of land.

  • Schools. The Wausau School District runs 14 elementary schools, John Muir and Horace Mann middle schools, and Wausau East and Wausau West high schools. The D.C. Everest Area School District also serves a large part of the Wausau area, so check which district a particular address belongs to.
  • Recreation. Rib Mountain State Park, Granite Peak Ski Area, the Leigh Yawkey Woodson Art Museum and the Grand Theater are the attractions the city is known for.
  • Jobs. Nearly a third of the Marathon County economy is manufacturing, with paper, insurance, home manufacturing and tourism among the prominent industries.
  • Transit and air. Metro Ride provides local buses, and Central Wisconsin Airport offers commercial flights with American Eagle and Delta Connection.
  • Nearby communities. Schofield, Weston, Mosinee, Maine, Rib Mountain, Kronenwetter and Rothschild form the suburban ring.

Personal representatives, trustees and court-appointed fiduciaries who never occupied the home do not have to complete it.

The grantor also pays a transfer fee of 30 cents per $100 of value under s. 77.22, or $3 per $1,000, collected when the deed is recorded. A Wausau home sold for $170,000 would owe $510. Both grantor and grantee sign the electronic return, and transfers by will, descent or survivorship are among those exempted by s. 77.25.

How do property taxes and assessments work in Wausau?

Wausau taxes are due in full by January 31 or in installments on January 31, April 30 and July 31, and special assessment charges on the bill must be paid in full by January 31. The city clerk's office handles these payments directly, and Marathon County says payments for the City of Wausau are not made to the county. Pay online through ePayments, by ACH, at participating banks until July 31, in the drop boxes at City Hall on Grant Street or across from the post office on Forest Street, by mail, or in person at 407 Grant Street between 8:00 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. A returned electronic payment carries a $45 fee.

The Assessment Department at 715-261-6600 values property under chapter 70 of the Wisconsin Statutes at the full value obtainable in a private sale. The city's last revaluation was as of January 1, 2020, and the state compares assessments to sales to see whether the citywide ratio stays between 90 and 110 percent of market value. You get a mailed notice when your assessment changes, and the Open Book period lets you meet an appraiser before any formal appeal.

Sellers who are behind on taxes may find help close to home. Marathon County lists a 5x5 short-term loan of up to $5,000 for taxes that are three years or more past due, open to applicants who are 55 or older or disabled, with a $3 monthly service charge. Call the county at 715-261-1150 to ask about eligibility.

Which Wausau city rules matter before I list?

Property maintenance and rental rules are the two areas most likely to affect a sale. The Inspections and Zoning division, at 407 Grant Street and 715-261-6780, handles complaints and permits. Its rules cover trash containers, parked vehicles and yard signs, and a buyer's agent walking the property will notice any violation.

  • Trash and recycling carts may go out no sooner than 3:00 p.m. the day before pickup and must be removed by 11:00 a.m. the day after. Between pickups they belong in a garage, shed, or behind or beside the house.
  • Vehicles may be parked only on hard-surfaced driveway areas, not on the grass. Inoperative or unlicensed vehicles are not allowed on residential lots.
  • Boats, trailers, campers and similar equipment cannot sit in a required front yard or corner side yard except on a hard-surfaced driveway, and anything over 30 feet must be in an enclosed structure.
  • Zoning allows two yard signs at a time, each no larger than 6 square feet and 4 feet high. Real estate signs cannot be placed on boulevards, public right-of-way or utility poles.

If the house is a rental, the division's rental properties page lists rental registration, rental licensing and inspection, and a rent abatement program. Ask the division which of those apply to your unit before you transfer it.

How do I record the deed in Marathon County?

Mail the original deed, the electronic transfer return receipt and the recording fee to the Register of Deeds at 500 Forest Street, Wausau. The fee is $30 per document, and any transfer fee is paid at the same time. Since January 1, 2026 the office returns recorded documents electronically unless you include a self-addressed, stamped envelope, so write your email address on the submission.

The county cannot give legal advice. A title company or an attorney commonly prepares the deed. The recorded-document certification fee is $1 and copies cost $2 for the first page and $1 for each additional page.

  • Accept a cash offer. Fits an inherited house, a rental with tenants, a house with deferred repairs, or a seller on a short clock. Ask for the number in writing and for who pays title and recording costs.

The Marathon County Register of Deeds charges $30 per document, plus any real estate transfer fee shown on the electronic return receipt. Copies are $2 for the first page and $1 for each additional page. Documents go to 500 Forest Street, Wausau.

When are Wausau property taxes due?

Pay in full by January 31, or in installments due January 31, April 30 and July 31. Special assessment charges on the bill must be paid in full by January 31. The City of Wausau collects these payments, not Marathon County.

Yes, for one-to-four unit homes. Wis. Stat. chapter 709 requires the completed report within 10 days after the contract is accepted. A buyer who does not get it may rescind within two business days after that period, unless you are an exempt fiduciary who never lived in the home.

Can I put a for-sale sign in my Wausau yard?

Yes, on your own property. Zoning allows two yard signs at one time, each up to 6 square feet and 4 feet tall. Signs cannot be placed on boulevards, other public right-of-way or utility poles.

The local market

Eastern Waukesha County holds New Berlin, a Milwaukee-area city of 39,953 people. Owners live in about 76.5 percent of homes, and 23.6 percent of residents are 65 or older. Many houses have been in one family for years and show it in layers of renovation. For those, gather permit history early, because a buyer's inspector may want to match kitchens, decks and furnaces to permit records.

A median owner-occupied value of $365,700 comes from a survey of every owner-occupied home. What yours sells for depends on its condition, its lot and when you list.

School districts and your tax bill

Four districts serve the city between them: Elmbrook, Muskego-Norway, New Berlin, and West Allis-West Milwaukee. The Schools page on the city's site lists all four and the private schools.

Your tax rate depends on which district your parcel is in. The city's Tax Levies and Rates page breaks out each one. Find the district on your own bill first, because parents shopping for a home usually ask about it before anything else.

City permits and utility bills

Community Development, on the second floor of City Hall at 3805 S. Casper Drive, is the place to begin. Permit applications are accepted Monday through Friday, 8:00 am to 4:00 pm. Inspectors cover the front counter from 8:00 to 9:00 am on weekdays, and reviewing a building permit may take up to 10 business days.

A buyer's inspector may compare the following kinds of past work with permit records.

  • New or replacement furnaces, air conditioners and water heaters
  • Decks, whether attached or detached, plus garages, sheds and similar accessory buildings
  • Kitchen remodels, additions, alterations and recreation rooms
  • Generators, hot tubs, pools and solar panels
  • Razing of a structure

If you cannot tell whether earlier work had a permit, phone Community Development before you list.

Water, sewer and stormwater bills also surface at closing. Wis. Disclosure duties under state law

Wis. Stat. 709.02 applies to homes of one to four units. You prepare a Real Estate Condition Report, and the buyer has to get it by day 10 after acceptance. A late report gives the buyer a way out: two business days after day 10 to rescind and recover deposits.

The report is a disclosure and promises nothing about the house. Court-appointed fiduciaries who never lived there are excused by Wis. Stat. 709.01, and so are transfers exempt from the transfer fee. Suppose you learn something after finishing the report but before the buyer accepts. Wis. Stat. 709.035 then asks for an amended report within 10 days of acceptance. Fill in every line, since an unanswered item leaves the report incomplete.

Cash buyers trim the start of this timeline, since no appraisal or loan approval sits between acceptance and closing. The report, return and recording all stay.

Documents to line up

Pull together what a title company will ask for before buyers start calling. Your tax bill gives the parcel number. Your lender supplies a payoff figure. Add permit records for earlier work, the name of your school district, and water, sewer and stormwater account details so the last bill closes out cleanly. When a deceased spouse is still on title, include the HT-110 form, a transfer return receipt and a copy of the document showing the interest.

Next, have every buyer or agent answer the same three questions in writing: when will we close, what fees come out of my proceeds, and what happens if the inspection finds a problem. Written answers make offers easy to compare. Keep every quote, because a cash buyer's figure and an agent's net after commission only line up when both are on paper.

Yes, ask for it in the contract. Many cash buyers work that way. You still owe a condition report unless an exemption fits, due within 10 days of acceptance.

The seller, as grantor, at 30 cents per $100 of value under Wis. Stat. 77.22. The register collects it at recording, and any other closing charges are for the contract to settle.

How long until I get my recorded deed back from Waukesha County?

Immediately for an e-recorded deed. A paper deed comes back right away if you gave a valid email address, or in two to three weeks by mail with a stamped return envelope.

What paperwork follows a co-owner's death?

File form HT-110 with a transfer return receipt, a copy of the document showing the decedent's interest and a $30 check or money order. Confirm details with the office or an attorney.

What are the ways to sell a house in West Bend, Wisconsin?

A West Bend homeowner can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept an offer from a cash buyer. All three routes end the same way: a deed recorded with the Washington County Register of Deeds and a transfer return filed with the state.

The right route depends on the condition of the house and how soon you need to close.

  • Listing with an agent suits a house in good repair when you can wait through showings, a buyer's inspection and a buyer's loan approval.
  • Selling on your own saves the agent's fee but leaves pricing, paperwork and negotiation with you.
  • A cash offer suits a house that needs work, an inherited West Bend property, or a sale where the closing date matters more than the last dollar of price.

Whichever route you take, ask for the terms in writing and compare what you would net after the transfer fee, any tax owed and repairs.

What is West Bend like for a home seller?

West Bend is the county seat of Washington County and part of the Milwaukee metropolitan area. The Census Bureau estimated 32,268 residents on July 1, 2025, up from 31,752 at the 2020 census.

The city began in 1845, when commissioners chose a westward bend in the Milwaukee River for a settlement because the river could power mills. West Bend became a village in 1868 and a city in 1885, and it annexed the Village of Barton on November 1, 1961. Between 1950 and 1990 the population grew from 6,849 to 23,916 as US 45 made it practical to live in West Bend and work elsewhere. A house built in that postwar growth is now several decades old, which is why buyers look hard at the roof, furnace and basement.

The local economy grew from manufacturing and financial services; West Bend Mutual Insurance was founded in the city in 1894. Many residents now work in neighboring communities. Buyers also notice the outdoors: the Riverwalk along the Milwaukee River, the Eisenbahn State Trail, the Ice Age Trail, Regner Park, Quaas Creek Park and the 137-acre Lac Lawrann Conservancy. A farmers' market runs in downtown West Bend on Saturday mornings from May through October.

How does West Bend weather and terrain affect a house?

West Bend has cold, snowy winters, so the heating system and roof draw the most attention from buyers. The average July high is 81 degrees F and the average January low is 11 degrees F. The city averages 31.4 inches of rain and 45.6 inches of snow a year.

The city sits in the Kettle Moraine region, where glaciers left kettles and hills. Hilly ground can bring runoff toward a foundation, so note any grading or drainage work you have done.   • Furnace and air conditioner age and service records.

Which roads and schools do West Bend buyers ask about?

Buyers ask about the West Bend School District and the route to Milwaukee. The district's own site says West Bend East and West High Schools will consolidate into a single West Bend High School for the 2027-2028 school year, and it reports that its elementary schools earn Significantly Exceeds or Exceeds Expectations on the Wisconsin DPI Report Card. It also offers 4K at seven locations and 30 Advanced Placement classes.

For commuting, West Bend is served by US 45 as a freeway bypass west of downtown, Wisconsin 33 and Wisconsin 144. A city-owned municipal airport sits east of downtown. The Washington County Commuter Express bus to Milwaukee ended in 2023, so most commuters drive; the Census Bureau puts the average trip to work at 25.9 minutes.

What City of West Bend permits matter before you sell?

Work done without a permit can slow a sale, so check your permit history with the City of West Bend Building Inspection office at (262) 335-5140. The office says permits must be obtained before any building activity begins, and inspections are scheduled within 24 to 48 hours of a request.

According to the city's FAQ, a permit is required for each of these:

  • Finishing a basement, remodeling living space, adding a dormer, an addition or a three-season room.
  • Adding or replacing a deck or porch.
  • Replacing roofing or siding.
  • Installing a shed, fence, driveway or swimming pool.
  • Replacing a furnace or air conditioner.

Detached garages and other accessory structures are capped at 720 square feet in total, and a detached garage at 18 feet in height. The owner and occupant of a single-family home may do their own electrical and plumbing work with a permit. Duplex and condo owners may not, and no homeowner may work on the electrical service to the home or on a pool or spa. If a past owner skipped a permit, ask the office what it would take to close it out before a buyer's inspector finds it.

What does recording a deed in Washington County cost?

Recording a deed costs $30 for most documents, and the seller pays a state transfer fee of 30 cents for each $100 of value. The recording fee comes from Wis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag) and the transfer fee from Wis. Stat. 77.22(1), which is $3 per $1,000.

As an example, a sale at $263,100, the Census median for West Bend, carries a transfer fee of about $789. The register collects the fee when the deed is submitted, and a completed real estate transfer return, filed electronically with the Department of Revenue, must accompany the deed. The Washington County Register of Deeds can be reached at 262-335-4320.

Some transfers carry no fee. Under Wis. Stat. 77.25, exemptions include:

  • A transfer by will, descent or survivorship.
  • A foreclosure deed, or a deed in lieu of foreclosure, to a mortgage holder.
  • A transfer between parent and child, stepparent and stepchild, or grandparent and grandchild for nominal or no consideration.
  • A transfer of real estate worth $1,000 or less.

The county also runs LandNotification, a free alert that emails you when a document is recorded under a name or parcel you choose. Recording a document does not by itself transfer ownership, and an alert lets you catch a false filing early.

How are property taxes handled when a West Bend house sells?

Property tax on a West Bend house is billed in arrears and is usually prorated between buyer and seller at closing. Wisconsin bills go out by the third Monday in December, and under Wis. Stat. 74.11 real property tax is paid in two equal installments, due January 31 and July 31, unless the whole bill is under $100, in which case it is due in full by January 31.

A first installment that is not received within five working days after January 31 makes the whole unpaid balance delinquent as of February 1. A seller who has not paid should ask the Washington County treasurer for the current balance, interest included, so the title company can pay it from proceeds.

If you live in the house, the lottery and gaming credit may appear on your bill. The Department of Revenue says that credit stays with the property when it sells, so the credit should be counted when taxes are prorated. A buyer who will live there files a new application.

How is the transfer fee figured on a West Bend sale?

Multiply the sale price by 0.30 percent. The fee is 30 cents for each $100 of value or fraction of $100, so a $200,000 sale carries a $600 fee. The register of deeds collects it when the deed is submitted for recording.

Who pays the transfer fee in West Bend?

The seller pays it. Wis. Stat. 77.22(1) places the fee on the grantor of the real estate, and the Washington County Register of Deeds collects it at recording.

Can I do my own electrical or plumbing work on my West Bend house?

Yes, if you own and live in a single-family home, and you still need a permit. The City of West Bend says duplex and condo owners may not do their own work, and no homeowner may touch the electrical service or work on a swimming pool or spa.

Does the lottery credit go to the buyer of my West Bend house?

The credit stays with the property. The Department of Revenue says it is deducted from the next tax bill and should be counted when taxes are prorated, and a buyer who will live in the house files a new application.

How can I watch for deed fraud on my West Bend property?

Sign up for the Washington County LandNotification alert, which emails you when a document is recorded under your name or parcel. The county notes that recording a document does not automatically transfer ownership, and it advises reporting suspected fraud to law enforcement and your title insurer.

Apply first to Development Services with a $100 fee. Once approved, the Health Department's sanitarian explains the license process, and no rental is allowed until the pre-inspection is done.

A house with a short-term rental history should have its license status confirmed with Development Services before listing, because a buyer planning the same use will ask.

Recording a deed in Brown County

The office is in the Northern Building, Room 260, 305 E. Walnut Street, Green Bay (920-448-4470). It is open 7:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday to Thursday and 7:30 to 11:30 a.m. on Friday, and it takes walk-in real estate recordings until 4:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday and until 10:30 a.m. Friday.

Tag-less recording is now standard. If you file on paper, you also submit a Swift Agreement and then get an email with a secure link good for up to three printed copies over seven days.

The deed needs a state transfer return as well. Wis. Stat. 77.22 puts the grantor on the hook for 30 cents per $100 of value, with the return filed electronically. The fee is noted on the face of the deed, and an exempt sale must state its reason there.

What a De Pere seller must disclose

Chapter 709 reaches sales, exchanges and land contracts for one to four dwelling units and for vacant land, but not dwellings never lived in. Owners fill out the state's condition report and deliver it within 10 days of contract acceptance.

If the report is late, the buyer gets a short window to cancel. Heirs selling an estate house are often covered by the exception for personal representatives, trustees and conservators who never lived there. Other sellers should answer every item, since a partly filled report is incomplete.

From contract to closing in De Pere

  6. File the electronic transfer return, then record the deed in Green Bay.

If an assessor letter or Open Book question arrives while the house is under contract, call the assessor and keep the buyer informed, since open book is a quick and informal way to settle a value question. After closing, tell the treasurer the new mailing address so bills reach the right owner.

Listing or cash sale?

Listing works for a house that shows well and a seller who can wait for a buyer's loan. A cash sale works for open permits, deferred maintenance, tenants or an estate to close out.

Ask for a net sheet either way, covering the loan payoff, the transfer fee, recording, prorated taxes and repair credits, so you compare what you would actually receive. Add the Brown County Treasurer's tax balance and any open permit items to that sheet, and settle them before the closing date.

Accurate Appraisal, LLC of Menasha, under contract with the city. De Pere has assessed every property annually since 2018, and owners can attend an Open Book session to discuss a value.

The Brown County Register of Deeds in Green Bay, 920-448-4470, which requires a Swift Agreement with paper filings.

Residential and commercial permits come from the village Building Department, which employs building, electrical and plumbing inspectors. The state's online system handles permits for new homes, while plumbing and electrical permits are separate from the main application.

The Mequon Water Utility supplies Mequon, Thiensville and Bayside, but a good number of homes continue to rely on a private well or a water trust.

The utility reports no lead water mains and no lead service lines, and plastic laterals have been required since service began in 1998. If yours is an older house, an inspector may point at those fixtures.
